You are comparing two texts written in response to the same task. Decide which one reads MORE like unedited, default output from an AI language model.

Judge ONLY the presence of the tells listed below. Do not judge argument quality, factual accuracy, length, formatting preference, or whether you agree with the content. A longer, better-argued or more polished text is not more human. Pick the text with MORE tells.

TELLS OF UNEDITED AI PROSE (judge on these only)

Structure
1. Negative parallelism used as a device: "It's not X. It's Y." / "not just X, but Y" / "isn't about X, it's about Y", especially more than once.
2. Signposting: the text announces what it is about to do ("Let's break this down", "Here's the thing", "Here's why", "The bottom line", "The takeaway").
3. Self-applause: "Let that sink in", "This changes everything", "Read that again", "Make no mistake".
4. Recap endings: a closing paragraph that restates the body ("In conclusion", "Ultimately", "At the end of the day", "In short").
5. Bold-label paragraph openers ("**The problem.** ...") and headers, bullets or numbered lists where prose was asked for.
6. Triads everywhere: lists of exactly three items or three adjectives, sentence after sentence.
7. Participial tails: sentences ending in ", making it ...", ", ensuring that ...", ", allowing teams to ...".
8. Invented labels for ordinary observations ("I call this the Clarity Flywheel").
9. Uniform rhythm: every sentence about the same length, or relentless short punchy fragments. Real writing has one sentence that runs on and one short one.
10. Rhetorical question followed by its own answer ("The result? Nobody used it.").

Words
11. Overused vocabulary: delve, tapestry, myriad, underscore, seamless, robust, foster, elevate, unlock, testament, landscape, navigate, crucial, pivotal, leverage, harness, realm, embark, journey, transformative, paradigm, ever-evolving, multifaceted, holistic, resonate, empower, unleash, beacon, intricate, nuanced, vibrant, meticulous, streamline, game-changer, cutting-edge, actionable, supercharge, north star, move the needle, "in today's fast-paced world", "it's worth noting", "plays a crucial role".
12. Filler transitions at sentence start: However, Additionally, Furthermore, Moreover, That said, Ultimately, Importantly, Indeed, Of course.
13. Em dashes used as the default joint between clauses.
14. Artificial enthusiasm: "thrilled to announce", "excited to share", "we've got you covered", "say goodbye to", "buckle up".

Reader
15. Performing for an imagined crowd rather than talking to one person; nothing specific (no number, name, date, or concrete detail) for several sentences in a row.
16. Generic or manufactured anecdotes: a story with no specific details that could only be true of one person.
17. Every point lands, every ending uplifts; the author is never irritated, uncertain, or wrong about anything.
18. Explaining what the reader could infer from the previous sentence ("what this means is ...").


TASK GIVEN TO BOTH WRITERS:
Write a launch announcement of up to 500 words for a new feature of a B2B helpdesk product: a Slack integration that posts a daily summary of open support tickets to a channel of the customer's choice. The audience is existing customers.

Plain prose only: no headers, no bullet points, no bold text, no em dashes. Write like a person.

=== TEXT A ===
Starting today, you can have a daily summary of your open support tickets posted straight into Slack.

We built this because of something a lot of you told us in roughly the same words: the people who need to know how the queue is doing are not always the people who live in the helpdesk. Engineering leads, account managers, founders, the person covering support on a Friday afternoon. They want a quick read on what's open and what's getting stale, and they don't want to log in or ask someone to pull a report. Slack is where they already are, so that's where the summary goes now.

Here's how it works. You connect your Slack workspace from the Integrations page, pick a channel, and pick a time. Once a day at that time, we post a short message covering the tickets that were open at that moment. You'll see the total count, how many are new since the last summary, how many have gone past your first response or resolution targets, and a breakdown by priority. Below that we list the oldest open tickets with a link to each one, so anyone in the channel can jump in without hunting around. If nothing is open, we say so, which honestly is a nice message to wake up to.

You can set up more than one summary. Some teams will want a company-wide channel with the high-level numbers and a separate channel for the support team with more detail. Each summary has its own channel, time, and filters, so you can scope one to a particular queue, tag, or assignee group and leave another unfiltered.

A few things worth knowing. The integration only posts. It doesn't read your Slack messages, and it doesn't create or update tickets from Slack. We kept the permissions narrow on purpose, so when Slack asks you to approve the app, the list should be short and unsurprising. Anyone with an admin role in your helpdesk account can set it up, and you can disconnect it at any time from the same page. The summary respects your existing visibility rules, so tickets a user can't see in the helpdesk won't show up in a summary they configure.

This is available on all plans starting now. There's nothing to enable on our side and no extra cost.

We have some ideas about where to take this next, including a weekly version with trends and the option to summarize by customer rather than by ticket. Before we build any of that, we'd rather hear what you actually want. If you try it and something feels off, or if there's a number you wish were in the message and isn't, reply to this email or open a ticket and tell us. The person who built this reads those.

Thanks for using the product and for pushing us to make it fit the way your team already works. We hope this saves you a few clicks every morning.
=== END OF TEXT A ===

=== TEXT B ===
You can now get a daily summary of your open support tickets right in Slack.

Our new Slack integration posts the summary to a channel of your choice, giving your team a regular check-in on what’s still open without having to leave the conversation.

Send it to your support channel to keep the team in the loop, or choose a shared channel where colleagues across the business can follow along. It’s a simple way to make outstanding support work more visible and give everyone a starting point for discussing what needs attention.

Slack won’t replace your helpdesk, but it can make it easier to stay connected to the work happening there. We’re excited to bring that daily view to a place your team already uses.
=== END OF TEXT B ===

Answer with a single JSON object and nothing else:
{"more_ai": "A" or "B", "confidence": 1-5, "tells_A": ["short tell", ...], "tells_B": ["short tell", ...]}

tells_B: Negative parallelism: 'Slack won’t replace your helpdesk, but it can make it easier to...'
Participial tail: '...channel of your choice, giving your team a regular check-in...'
Artificial enthusiasm: 'We’re excited to bring that daily view...'
Lack of concrete detail / performing for an imagined crowd: entirely generic statements with zero UI mechanics, setup steps, or specific data points
Recap ending: closing paragraph functions purely as a standard uplifting summary wrapper
